changeSet.author: mseaton
changeSet.comment: UHM-9341: Backfill obs.order_id on existing testOrderNumber obs written by pre-redesign pihapps. The old specimenCollectionEncounter.gsp wrote testOrderNumber obs without setting obs.order_id, so the new indexed order_id-based fulfiller encounter lookup cannot find those encounters. This sets obs.order_id by matching obs.value_text to orders.order_number, scoped to the testOrderNumber concept (UUID 393dec41-2fb5-428f-acfa-36ea85da6666). Safe to run on sites where no matching obs exist — affects 0 rows.
changeSet.sql: UPDATE obs o INNER JOIN orders ord ON ord.order_number = o.value_text AND ord.voided = 0 SET o.order_id = ord.order_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL AND o.voided = 0 AND o.value_text IS NOT NULL AND o.concept_id IN (SELECT concept_id FROM concept WHERE uuid = '393dec41-2fb5-428f-acfa-36ea85da6666');

changeSet.author: mseaton
changeSet.comment: Adds a covering index on orders for the Lab Order List query (order_type_id, fulfiller_status, voided, order_action, date_stopped, auto_expire_date, date_activated). Without this, only the single-column order_type_id index is available, which forces the database to scan and sort the entire order-type history before it can apply any other filter - this becomes very slow on installations with millions of orders. Making the index fully covering for this WHERE clause lets MySQL's optimizer choose it on its own, with no query hint required. Verified via EXPLAIN ANALYZE against a copy of an affected production database: the default Lab Order List query dropped from ~1.1s to single-digit milliseconds.

changeSet.author: mseaton
changeSet.comment: Adds a second Lab Order List index on orders (order_type_id, voided, order_action, date_activated), complementing orders_lab_order_list_covering above. That index wins when the fulfillment status filter is narrow (e.g. the default "awaiting/in fulfillment" worklist view) with no date bound. This one wins whenever a date range is applied (e.g. activatedOnOrAfter/activatedOnOrBefore), regardless of how broad the status filter is - by putting date_activated near the front of the index, MySQL can jump directly to the bounded date range instead of scanning the full order-type history. Verified via EXPLAIN ANALYZE against a copy of an affected production database with a broad status filter (including COMPLETED_FULFILLMENT) plus a date filter: query dropped from ~1.15s to well under 1ms.
